films.title: Spotlight
films.synopsis: Starring Michael Keaton, Mark Ruffalo, Rachel McAdams, Liev Schreiber, Brian d’Arcy James and Stanley Tucci, SPOTLIGHT tells the riveting true story of the Pulitzer Prize-winning Boston Globe investigation that would rock the city and cause a crisis in one of the world’s oldest and most trusted institutions. When the newspaper’s tenacious “Spotlight” team of reporters delve into allegations of abuse in the Catholic Church, their year-long investigation uncovers a decades-long cover-up at the highest levels of Boston’s religious, legal, and government establishment, touching off a wave of revelations around the world. Directed by Academy Award-nominee Tom McCarthy, SPOTLIGHT is a tense investigative thriller, tracing the steps to one of the biggest crime stories in modern times.
films.after_screening: Post screening panel discussion with Martin Baron, Michael Rezendes, Sacha Pfeiffer, Walter Robinson, moderated by David Simon.

films.title: The True Cost
films.synopsis:
This is a story about clothing. It’s about the clothes we wear, the people who make them, and the impact the industry is having on our world. The price of clothing has been decreasing for decades, while the human and environmental costs have grown dramatically. THE TRUE COST is a groundbreaking documentary film that pulls back the curtain on the untold story and asks us to consider, who really pays the price for our clothing?

Filmed in countries all over the world, from the brightest runways to the darkest slums, and featuring interviews with the world’s leading influencers including Stella McCartney, Livia Firth and Vandana Shiva, THE TRUE COST is an unprecedented project that invites us on an eye opening journey around the world and into the lives of the many people and places behind our clothes.
films.after_screening: Post screening panel discussion with Scott Hahn, Rachel Louise Snyder and Margaret Talbot.

films.title: Cartel Land
films.synopsis:
With unprecedented access, CARTEL LAND is a riveting, on-the-ground look at the journeys of two modern-day vigilante groups and their shared enemy – the murderous Mexican drug cartels. In the Mexican state of Michoacán, Dr. Jose Mireles, a small-town physician known as “El Doctor,” leads the Autodéfensas, a citizen uprising against the violent Knights Templar drug cartel that has wreaked havoc on the region for years. Meanwhile, in Arizona’s Altar Valley – a narrow, 52-mile-long desert corridor known as Cocaine Alley – Tim “Nailer” Foley, an American veteran, heads a small paramilitary group called Arizona Border Recon, whose goal is to stop Mexico’s drug wars from seeping across our border.

Filmmaker Matthew Heineman embeds himself in the heart of darkness as Nailer, El Doctor, and the cartel each vie to bring their own brand of justice to a society where institutions have failed. From executive producer Kathryn Bigelow (THE HURT LOCKER, ZERO DARK THIRTY), CARTEL LAND is a chilling, visceral meditation on the breakdown of order and the blurry line between good and evil. At the 2015 Sundance Film Festival, Heineman received both the Directing Award and Special Jury Award for Cinematography in the U.S. Documentary competition.
films.after_screening: Post screening panel discussion with Matt Heineman and Ray Suarez.

films.title: Deep Web
films.synopsis:
This movie gives the inside story of one of the the most important and riveting digital crime sagas of the century -- the arrest of Ross William Ulbricht, the convicted 30-year-old entrepreneur accused to be ‘Dread Pirate Roberts,’ creator and operator of online black market Silk Road. The film explores how the brightest minds and thought leaders behind the Deep Web are now caught in the crosshairs of the battle for control of a future inextricably linked to technology, with our digital rights hanging in the balance.

In addition to being the only film with exclusive access to the Ulbricht family, DEEP WEB features the core architects of the Deep Web; anarchistic cryptographers who developed the Deep Web’s tools for the military in the early 1990s; the dissident journalists and whistleblowers who immediately sought refuge in this seemingly secure environment; and the figures behind the rise of Silk Road, which combined the security of the Deep Web with the anonymity of cryptocurrency.
films.after_screening: Post screening panel discussion with Joshua Dratel.

films.title: The Storm Makers
films.synopsis:
Aya was a slave. At the age of 16, the young Cambodian peasant was sold to work as a maid in Malaysia, where she was exploited and beaten during two years without receiving any salary. Now that she has returned to her village just as poor as when she left, what is left of her humanity?

The Storm Makers traces modern-day slavery in Cambodia, by uncovering the fate of this young woman and following, in parallel, the daily lives of two human traffickers, a local recruiter and the head of a trafficking network. Cambodians call them « mey kechol »: the storm makers.

From the impoverished remote villages to the bustling urban centre of Phnom Penh, the film reveals a unique perspective on the exploitation of Cambodia’s rural population and questions what is the price of a life in a country experiencing uninhibited economic development.
films.after_screening: Post screening panel discussion with Sara Colm, Terry Fitzpatrick and Douglas Gillison.

films.title: Drone
films.synopsis:
Inside the secret CIA drone war. Intimate stories from the war on terror. People living under drones in Pakistan and drone pilots struggling with killing through joysticks in the U.S.

The film covers diverse and integral ground, from the recruitment of young pilots at gaming conventions and the re-definition of “going to war,” to the moral stance of engineers behind the technology, to world leaders giving the secret “green light” to engage in the biggest targeted killing program in history, to the people willing to stand up for civil liberties and accountability.

This is just the beginning. In the midst of fast advancement of technology and lagging international legislation, the film shows how drones change wars--and possibly our future.
films.after_screening: Post screening panel discussion with Tom Blanton, Sabrina Buchwalter, Mark Mazzetti, Scott Shane and Daniel Zwerdling.

films.title: (T)ERROR
films.synopsis: Saeed “Shariff” Torres, a counterterrorism informant for more than two decades, takes on what he swears is his last job for the FBI and invites filmmakers to follow his covert efforts to befriend a suspected jihadist - without informing his superiors. As surprising revelations emerge, not only about Torres’ past, but also about the increasingly murky ethical grounds of his present mission, (T)ERROR explores just how far we are going to prevent terror and the liberties we are sacrificing to get there.
films.after_screening: Post screening panel discussion with Eric Lichtblau and David Felix Sutcliffe.

films.synopsis: On March 8, 1971 a group of citizens broke into the FBI’s office in Media, PA, took hundreds of secret files, and shared them with the public. Johanna Hamilton’s compelling film 1971 is their story.
films.after_screening: The film screening will be followed by a rare opportunity to hear from the members of the Citizens’ Commission who carried out the break-in, and will discuss the ongoing issues of government overreach and first amendment rights that still occupy the public debate more than 40 years later.

sessions.title: A Case of Identity
sessions.description: Investigative journalist… Filmmaker… Visual storyteller… What do each of these identities mean for the way stories are told, for the role of the storyteller, for ethics and legal protections? As the boundaries between these crafts blur and collide, are the distinct identities vanishing as well, or are they more important than ever?

sessions.title: Access and Advocacy
sessions.description: Many investigative news reports and documentaries rely on government sources for facts and commentary. In the past, these exchanges were facilitated by certain standards for objective reporting. But such clear lines are harder to draw in today’s mix of traditional journalism, documentaries, advocacy media and other approaches. A bipartisan panel of current and former Congressional, Federal Agency and White House spokespeople will discuss the challenges and opportunities these changes present for government sources and those who cover them.

sessions.title: Truth to Power: Trapdoors
sessions.description: Journalists and filmmakers are increasingly taking on powerful corporate interests and institutions. What happens when the targets of investigations go after the investigator? What are the areas of vulnerability, and how can reporters and visual storytellers protect themselves?

sessions.title: Encryption Workshop
sessions.description: Do you find encryption more hassle than hero? This workshop will give you a basic toolkit for protecting the confidentiality of communications. Your sources will thank you.

sessions.title: Safety on the Frontlines
sessions.description: Pursuit of a story can put reporters and filmmakers at physical risk in the field. Navigating the balance between storytelling and personal safety can make the difference between getting the killer shot and living to tell the tale. This panel will explore essential training and preparation for entering an area of conflict, and the measures that reporters and filmmakers can take to protect themselves.

sessions.title: Meet the Broadcasters
sessions.description: Lightning talks from broadcasters on the kinds of work they’ve produced in the past, what they’re looking for going forward, and the best way to approach them with new stories and ideas.

sessions.title: From Print to Screen
sessions.description: Investigative stories that originated with the written word and were then reinterpreted for the screen. How much does the film rely on the original writing and how does the addition of the audio/visual component impact the story? Hear first-hand how such collaborations have worked and what was gained or lost in the transition for both the filmmakers and the journalists.

sessions.title: C#ns*rsh!p by Proxy
sessions.venue: Newseum, Knight Conference Center, Room A
sessions.description: It’s not only government action that can block public access to investigative reporting. Pre-publication smear campaigns, insurance issues, and the mere threat of litigation – whether realized or not – have sometimes sufficed to keep important stories away from the public eye. Hear about first-hand experiences and learn how to anticipate--and sometimes avert--potential minefields.

sessions.title: Dangerous Docs: a Report
sessions.venue: Newseum, Knight Conference Center, Room B
sessions.description: Non-fiction filmmakers often face aggressive attack from powerful individuals, governmental bodies, businesses and associations. The Center for Media & Social Impact at American University published a report funded by the John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation to quantify the risks, and research if these can they be mitigated to encourage more and better expression on the important issues of the day. Hear directly from the researchers as they discuss their findings and share their recommendations for enabling filmmakers to continue to tell truth to power.

sessions.title: Storytelling on the Cutting Edge
sessions.venue: Newseum, Knight Conference Center, Room A
sessions.description: Investigative journalism and visual storytelling are increasingly pushing the boundaries, borrowing from art, gaming, and even poetry to discover new forms of capturing once-inaccessible perspectives and experiences. How do non-traditional forms of storytelling reach and impact increasingly media-savvy audiences? Whether taking advantage of new technologies or putting a modern twist on classic communication forms, there are more ways than ever to tell a story – graphic novels, animation, virtual reality, poetry, and others yet to be discovered.

sessions.title: Meet the Funders
sessions.venue: Newseum, Knight Conference Center, Room B
sessions.description: Straight talk from the people who make it all possible. Lightning talks from leading funders of documentary filmmaking on their strategies, the kinds of projects they’ve supported in the past, and what they hope to achieve by investing in filmmaking in the future.

sessions.title: Meet the Online Platforms
sessions.venue: Newseum, Knight Conference Center, Room A
sessions.description: As the audiences shrink for deep dive investigations and longform stories told solely in words, news organizations are increasingly tapping a variety of media to convey complex stories. Hear from individuals who are at the forefront of this new wave of short form visual journalism.

sessions.title: Alex Gibney, in Conversation with Franklin Foer
sessions.venue: Newseum, Knight Conference Center, Room B
sessions.description: Award-winning filmmaker Alex Gibney has long bridged investigative journalism and filmmaking. He has tackled some of the most topical stories of our day, including political and corporate corruption, deception by sports figures, and sexual abuse in the Catholic church. His film Going Clear: Scientology and the Prison of Belief (2015) recently won three Emmys. Franklin Foer, an author and fellow at the New America Foundation, is a former editor of The New Republic.
related_films: Going Clear: Scientology and the Prison of Belief

sessions.title: Crossing Boundaries, then and now: A Case Study of 1971 featuring activists of “the burglary” and Edward Snowden
sessions.venue: Newseum, Knight Conference Center, Room A
sessions.description: On March 8, 1971 a group of citizens broke into the FBI’s office in Media, PA, took hundreds of secret files, and shared them with the public. Johanna Hamilton’s compelling film 1971 is their story. The film screening will be followed by a rare opportunity to hear from the members of the Citizens’ Commission who carried out the break-in, and will discuss the ongoing issues of government overreach and first amendment rights that still occupy the public debate more than 40 years later.

people.name: Debra Anderson
people.bio: Debra Anderson, a digital media, strategy and marketing consultant, is a founding partner of the PeaceTechLab, in collaboration with INCORE at the University of Ulster. In 2013, she created, and taught, the first Big Data Consumer Research course at The New School for Public Engagement.

people.name: Raney Aronson-Rath
people.bio: Raney Aronson-Rath, executive producer of Frontline, PBS’ flagship investigative journalism series, has been internationally recognized for her work to re-imagine the documentary form across multiple media platforms. Aronson-Rath has developed and managed more than a dozen journalistic partnerships with news outlets including ProPublica, PBS Marketplace, PBS NewsHour, The New York Times, and CBC Television.

people.name: Patricia Aufderheide
people.bio: Patricia Aufderheide who teaches at the School of Communication at American University, is the founder-director of the Center for Media & Social Impact. Aufderheide currently sits on the board of directors of the Independent Television Service, which produces innovative television programming for underserved audiences under the umbrella of the Corporation for Public Broadcasting.
people.affiliation: Center for Media & Social Impact, American University

people.name: Kasia Cieplak-Mayr von Baldegg
people.bio: Kasia Cieplak-Mayr von Baldegg is the executive producer for video at The Atlantic. She joined the magazine in 2011 to launch its video channel and, in 2013, created its in-house video production department. Previously, she worked as a producer at Al Gore’s Current TV and as a content strategist and documentary producer in San Francisco.

people.name: Catherine Beck
people.bio: Catherine Beck is an award-winning member of the investigative reporting team at WXIA in Atlanta. Previously, she did similar work at WTVR in Richmond, VA. She has also taught broadcast writing at Virginia Commonwealth University.

people.name: Lowell Bergman
people.bio: Lowell Bergman is the Reva and David Logan Distinguished Chair in Investigative Reporting at the Graduate School of Journalism at UC Berkeley and director of the Investigative Reporting Program, where he has taught a seminar dedicated to investigative reporting for more than 20 years. He is also a producer/correspondent for the PBS documentary series Frontline.
people.affiliation: Graduate School of Journalism, UC Berkeley

people.name: Brian Boyer
people.bio: Brian Boyer is the visuals editor at NPR. Before NPR, he interned with ProPublica and then founded the news applications team at Chicago Tribune. He was one of the first two programmers to receive a Knight News Challenge-funded scholarship to study journalism at Medill. He loves his job.

people.name: Bruce D. Brown
people.bio: Bruce D. Brown, the executive director of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, co-directs the First Amendment Clinic at the University of Virginia Law School and is an adjunct professor at Georgetown University in its master’s program in journalism.
people.affiliation: Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press

people.name: John Cardellino
people.bio: John Cardellino is a senior consultant for the Sundance Documentary Film Program. Prior to his role as a consultant, Cardellino worked directly with filmmakers funded by the program, managing its creative labs and artist support programs while providing strategic and creative support to DFP grantees.

people.name: Caty Borum Chattoo
people.bio: Caty Borum Chattoo is a social-change communication specialist and media produce, who currently is an executive in residence at the School of Communication at American University. She has produced numerous film and television documentaries and multiple PSA campaigns.

people.name: Cindy Cohn
people.bio: Cindy Cohn, an attorney specializing in Internet law, became executive director of the Electronic Frontier Foundation in 2015 after serving 15 years as its legal director. Some of Cohn’s significant cases include Hepting v. AT&T, a class action against AT&T for collaborating with the National Security Agency to wiretap and data-mine Americans’ communications.

people.name: Christina Coleman
people.bio: Christina Coleman, anchor-reporter at KSDK TV in St. Louis, covered events in Ferguson, MO, for months after the shooting death of Michael Brown. She has also worked in Texas and Alaska.

people.name: Brenda Coughlin
people.bio: Brenda Coughlin was a producer of the documentary feature Citizenfour, a 2015 Academy Award winner. Coughlin is currently producing Asylum, a short-form episodic series about WikiLeaks, also directed by Laura Poitras, and “Astro Noise,” Poitras’ forthcoming solo exhibition at the Whitney Museum of American Art.

people.name: Robert Cribb
people.bio: Robert Cribb is an award-winning investigative reporter at the Toronto Star. He has received national reporting awards and citations for investigations into child exploitation, human trafficking, dangerous doctors and public-health threats.

people.name: Emma Dessau
people.bio: Emma Dessau is the senior producer of POV Digital, the Webby Award-winning department that drives storytelling innovation for the PBS documentary series POV. She also helps run the POV Hackathon Lab. Dessau co-produced two nonfiction projects, Folk to Folk, and The Story Store. She previously worked at Emerson College’s Engagement Game Lab in Boston.

people.name: Kirby Dick
people.bio: Kirby Dick’s most recent film, The Hunting Ground, an exposé about sexual assault on college campuses, premiered at the 2015 Sundance Film Festival and will have its television premiere on CNN this fall. His previous film, The Invisible War, an investigation into rape within the US military, won two Emmy Awards, a Peabody Award, and was nominated for an Academy Award.

people.name: Sky Dylan-Robbins
people.bio: Sky Dylan-Robbins is an award-winning video journalist at The New Yorker magazine. Previously, she was part of a small editorial team at Tumblr, the blogging platform. Dylan-Robbins graduated cum laude from Northwestern University with degrees in film, Italian and sociology, and has lived and worked in Bologna and Rome. She’s from — and still lives in — New York City.

people.name: Alisia Essig
people.bio: Alisia Essig was a legislative aide and communications director for Utah Congressman Jason Chaffetz from 2008 to 2011. Since then Essig has worked for Mia Love’s 2012 and 2014 congressional campaigns in Utah’s fourth district. Essig managed all local and national media requests as Love’s press secretary during both election

people.name: Andrew Feinstein
people.bio: Andrew Feinstein, a former ANC Member of Parliament in South Africa, is the author of After the Party: Corruption, the ANC and South Africa’s Uncertain Future, and The Shadow World: Inside the Global Arms Trade. He is the writer on the feature documentary of Shadow World, which will premiere in early 2016. Feinstein lives in London.

people.name: Franklin Foer
people.bio: Franklin Foer is a fellow at the New America Foundation. For seven years, he was the editor of the New Republic. He is the author of the international bestseller How Soccer Explains the World. Currently, he’s writing a book about Silicon Valley

people.name: Alex Gibney
people.bio: Alex Gibney received a Best Feature-Length Documentary Oscar in 2008 for Taxi to the Dark Side, a Best Director nomination from the Directors Guild of America, and a Writer’s Guild award for Best Screenplay. Gibney received an Academy Award nomination in 2006 for Enron: The Smartest Guys in the Room.

people.name: Johanna Hamilton
people.bio: Johanna Hamilton co-produced Pray the Devil Back to Hell, about women demanding peace for Liberia, which won the Grand Jury Prize for Best Documentary at the 2008 Tribeca Film Festival. In Fall 2011, it led the PBS mini-series Women, War & Peace, which won the Overseas Press Club Edward R. Murrow Award for best documentary. The film 1971 is her documentary feature debut.

people.name: Laura Handman
people.bio: Laura Handman, a partner at the law firm of Davis Wright Tremaine, has extensive experience in libel, newsgathering, privacy, right of publicity, reporter’s privilege and First Amendment matters. She obtained the first decision in U.S. courts refusing to enforce foreign libel judgments as inconsistent with the First Amendment.

people.name: Matthew Heineman
people.bio: Matthew Heineman’s latest film CARTEL LAND premiered in the U.S. Documentary Competition at the 2015 Sundance Film Festival, where Heineman won the Best Director Award and Special Jury Prize for Cinematography. The film will be released in theatres in the Fall of 2015 and have it’s broadcast premiere on A&E in 2016.

people.name: Harlo Holmes
people.bio: Harlo Holmes is a digital security trainer. She helps journalists in various media organizations become confident and effective in securing their communications within their newsrooms, with their sources, and with the public at large. She is a media scholar, software programmer, and activist; and contributes regularly to the open source mobile security collective, The Guardian Project.

people.name: Kathy Im
people.bio: Kathy Im oversees investments in the John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation’s journalism program. On sabbatical from the foundation, she explored the intersection of interactive documentaries and digital journalism at MIT. Prior to joining the foundation, Im worked at the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development and the Bank of America Foundation.
people.affiliation: John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation

people.name: Will Jenkins
people.bio: Will Jenkins has, for nearly a decade, worked in communications and policy at the White House, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, and both houses of Congress. Over the years, he has worked with dozens of filmmakers to help them understand and engage the policymaking process. He also wrote a guide to politics for filmmakers for Documentary magazine.

people.name: Kirsten Johnson
people.bio: Kirsten Johnson is a cinematographer and director whose camerawork appeared in Citizenfour, which won the Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature at the 2015 Oscars. Johnson teaches “Visual Thinking” at the Graduate Journalism Department at NYU and cinematography in the Masters in Film program at the School of Visual Arts.

people.name: Brenda Jones
people.bio: Brenda Jones, communications director for Rep. John Lewis for 11 years, has worked with Hollywood film producers, documentary film and radio producers, and many TV, radio, and print journalists to tell the congressman’s story. She began her career in public broadcasting and radio and had stints in commercial TV at CBS and ABC networks.

people.name: David Kairys
people.bio: David Kairys, a law professor at Temple University, specializes in constitutional law and civil rights law. He has won numerous awards for his work, including the Alliance for Justice honor list for 2008 and the Association of American Law Schools 2007 Deborah Rhode Award for extraordinary contribution to public interest by a law professor.

people.name: Cynthia Kane
people.bio: Cynthia Kane works as senior commissioning producer in Al Jazeera America’s Doc Unit. Previously, she was at ITVS (Independent Television Service) managing the international initiative for funding, and also supported the domestic funding initiatives. She worked at Sundance Channel and co-created DOCday during her 10-year tenure there.

people.name: Ross Kauffman
people.bio: Ross Kauffman was the director, producer, cinematographer and co-editor of Born into Brothels, which won a 2005 Oscar for Best Documentary. Kaufman’s current projects include Right on Red, a film about a gay couple trying to adopt a newborn baby from a drug-addicted woman and her abusive lesbian partner, and the documentary Wait For Me, chronicling a mother’s search for her son missing for 23 years.

people.name: Chris Kelly
people.bio: Chris Kelly has spent the last six years living in Cambodia filming the feature documentary, The Cause of Progress, which is in post-production now. His most recent film, Supermarket Slave Trail, which was produced for The Guardian, caused many supermarkets around the world to stop selling prawns farmed in Thailand. Kelly is the founder of production company Little Ease Films Ltd.

people.name: Brian Knappenberger
people.bio: Brian Knappenberger, a documentary producer and director, created We Are Legion: The Story of the Hacktivists, about the online hacktivist non-group Anonymous; Life After War, about political tensions in post-war Afghanistan; and A Murder in Kyiv, about the death of a Ukrainian journalist reportedly at the hands of government officials.

people.name: Dan Krauss
people.bio: Dan Krauss was nominated for an Academy Award and two Emmy Awards for his first film, The Death of Kevin Carter. His most recent film, The Kill Team, won The Grand Jury Prize for Best Documentary at the Tribeca Film Festival, the Truer than Fiction Independent Spirit Award and the National Board of Review Top 5. Krauss lectures at UC Berkeley’s Graduate School of Journalism on documentary film and television production.

people.name: Valerie Lapinski
people.bio: Valerie Lapinski is the head of video at Guardian US. She has previously worked in multimedia production at TIME, WNYC public radio and the New York Times.

people.name: Wendy Levy
people.bio: Wendy Levy is the Director of New Arts Axis. She is also a Senior Consultant with the Sundance Institute Documentary Film Program and the Co-Founder of Sparkwise, an online data and story platform funded by the MacArthur Foundation, Ford Foundation and Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation.

people.name: Charles Lewis
people.bio: Charles Lewis, a former ABC News and 60 Minutes producer, founded the Investigative Reporting Workshop and before that the Center for Public Integrity and its International Consortium of Investigative Journalists. Lewis recently helped create the Investigative News Network, comprised of more than 90 nonprofit news publishers. He is a professor at American University School of Communication.

people.name: Kathleen Lingo
people.bio: Kathleen Lingo is the coordinating producer of The New York Times’ Op-Doc series. Before joining The Times, she worked on news and documentary projects at HBO, IFC, WNYC, and Jigsaw Productions. Last year, she won an Emmy as part of the team for A Short History of the Highrise produced by The New York Times and the National Film Board of Canada.

people.name: Richard Logan
people.bio: Richard Logan is the founding executive of a UK-based Mac software company, and is president of The Reva and David Logan Foundation of Chicago. The foundation is a substantial program contributor to the Logan Center for the Arts at the University of Chicago and invests in investigative journalism in the U.S. and Europe.
people.affiliation: The Reva and David Logan Foundation

people.name: Carrie Lozano
people.bio: Carrie Lozano was until recently executive producer for documentaries at Al Jazeera America. Prior to that she was senior producer of the Emmy and Peabody Award winning series Fault Lines. She was also a contributing reporter on PBS Frontline’s Black Money and Post Mortem. She is currently producing and directing a documentary film about jazz pianist Fred Hersch.

people.name: Betty Medsger
people.bio: In 1971, Betty Medsger, then a Washington Post reporter, broke the story about FBI files stolen by anonymous burglars. Those files proved FBI director J. Edgar Hoover directed the agency to conduct dirty, violent tricks against civil rights and peace activists and African-Americans in general. In 2014, Medsger revealed her sources in her book, The Burglary: The Discovery of J. Edgar Hoover’s Secret FBI. She lives in New York.

people.name: Thor Neureiter
people.bio: Thor Neureiter is an independent documentary producer, cameraman and editor whose work focuses on US foreign policy and domestic politics. In 2012, Neureiter’s films Mitt Romney and the Mormon Factor and Prosecute Wall Street aired on Al Jazeera English. He has worked on programming for PBS and HBO.

people.name: Ron Nixon
people.bio: Ron Nixon is a Washington correspondent for the New York Times who covers federal regulatory agencies. He is the chairman of the board of 100Reporters and is author of the book Selling Apartheid: Apartheid South Africa’s Global Propaganda War (Jacana Media, June 2015).

people.name: Greg Norcie
people.bio: Greg Norcie is a staff technologist at the Center for Democracy and Technology. He provides technical expertise to assist CDT staff in formulating and articulating policy positions, and also works on CDT’s Internet Architecture project, where he focuses on embedding privacy and respect for human rights into technical standards and policy decisions.

people.name: Ricardo Sandoval Palos
people.bio: Ricardo Sandoval Palos is supervising editor of NPR’s Morning Edition. He also is president of the board of directors at the nonprofit Fund for Investigative Journalism. Before joining NPR, he edited international investigations for the Center for Public Integrity, and previously was a Latin America correspondent for the Dallas Morning News and Knight Ridder.

people.name: Nonny de la Peña
people.bio: Nonny de la Peña has built more than five virtual reality constructs including Hunger in Los Angeles, which premiered at the Sundance Film Festival in January 2012. She has been a correspondent for Newsweek Magazine and her work has appeared in the publications such the New York Times, Los Angeles Times Magazine, and Premiere Magazine.

people.name: Bonnie Raines
people.bio: Bonnie Raines is one of the “anonymous burglars” who broke into an FBI office in Media, Penn., in 1971 that led to Betty Medsger’s stories unmasking of J. Edgar Hoover. Today she is the mother of four and grandmother of seven who remains politically active.

people.name: John Raines
people.bio: John Raines has taught in the religion department at Temple University for the past 47 years. Raines, a “Freedom Rider” who was jailed in 1964, joined the anti-Vietnam movement. Eventually, he and his wife Bonnie became a part of The Citizens Commission to Investigate the FBI, which led to Betty Medsger’s revelations of civil rights violations.

people.name: Betsy Reed
people.bio: Betsy Reed is Editor-in-Chief of The Intercept. Previously, she was Executive Editor of The Nation, where she led the magazine’s award-winning investigative coverage. She has edited several bestselling books, including Jeremy Scahill’s Blackwater and Dirty Wars. Reed co-edited the New York Times bestseller Going Rouge: Sarah Palin –An American Nightmare.

people.name: Elspeth Revere
people.bio: Elspeth Revere is Vice President of Media, Culture, and Special Initiatives at the MacArthur Foundation. Her responsibilities at the foundation include “support for media in a technologically changing environment.. strengthening American democracy, arts and culture in Chicago, grants in response to special opportunities, and the Foundation’s program of institutional grants.”

people.name: James Risen
people.bio: James Risen is a The New York Times reporter who previously worked for the Los Angeles Times. He is the author or co-author of two books about the Central Intelligence Agency and a book about the American public debate about abortion. Risen is a two-time Pulitzer Prize winner.

people.name: Walter Robinson
people.bio: Walter Robinson, editor at large at the Boston Globe, has been a reporter and editor there for 43 years. He covered city, state and national politics and government, and was the newspaper’s Middle East correspondent during the First Gulf War. He led the investigation that exposed the Catholic Church’s cover-up of decades of sexual abuse by nearly 200 priests.

people.name: Diana Jean Schemo
people.bio: Diana Jean Schemo is co-founder and executive editor of 100Reporters, a nonprofit investigative news consortium, and founding director of the Double Exposure: The Investigative Film Festival and Symposium. Ms. Schemo is an author and former national and foreign correspondent at The New York Times and The Baltimore Sun.

people.name: Michael I. Schiller
people.bio: Michael I. Schiller is the creative director of Reveal for The Center for Investigative Reporting. His most recent short animated film, The Box, won first prize at the San Francisco International Film Festival and was honored at The Webbys, the New Orleans Film Festival and the Northern California Society of Professional Journalists.

people.name: Michael Shagoury
people.bio: Michael Shagoury is digital media professional and entrepreneur who is currently executive producer and acting editorial lead of AJ+. As a broadcast professional, he produced news and documentaries for CNN, Al Jazeera, BBC, ZDF and NBC. Shagoury spearheaded the establishment of the World Media Academy in Dubai, which trains broadcasting, print journalism and public relations professionals.

people.name: Edward Snowden
people.bio: Edward Snowden is a former National Security Agency subcontractor who made headlines in 2013 when he leaked top secret information about NSA surveillance activities.

people.name: Rachel Louise Snyder
people.bio: Rachel Louise Snyder, an associate professor in the MFA creative writing program and the journalism program at American University, has published both nonfiction and fiction books and written for numerous national magazines and newspapers. She hosted the nationally syndicated global affairs series “Latitudes” on public radio, and her stories have aired on Marketplace and All Things Considered.

people.name: Drew Sullivan
people.bio: Drew Sullivan founded the Center for Investigative Reporting in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 2004 and served as its editor and first director. Today he directs the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Program, an organization he founded together with journalists from a dozen countries. He has also served on the board.
people.affiliation: Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Program

people.name: David Felix Sutcliffe
people.bio: David Felix Sutcliffe’s film, (T)ERROR, co-directed with Lyric R. Cabral, debuted at the 2015 Sundance Film Festival where it won a Special Jury Prize, as well as the Grand Jury Prize at the 2015 Full Frame Film Festival. (T)ERROR will be released in theatres in the fall of 2015, followed by a U.S. and international broadcast in early 2016.

people.name: Margaret Talbot
people.bio: Margaret Talbot joined The New Yorker as a staff writer. Previously, she was a contributing writer at the New York Times Magazine and, from 1995 to 1999, an editor at The New Republic. She is the author of “The Entertainer: Movies, Magic and My Father’s Twentieth Century,” about Lyle Talbot, her father.

people.name: Katie Townsend
people.bio: Katie Townsend is the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press’ first litigation director. She oversees freedom of information activities and participates in a full range of media law issues with a focus on handling litigation brought by the Reporters Committee. Townsend, who holds a B.A in English and a B.S. in broadcast journalism, was a reporter and producer for a local AM news radio station as an undergraduate.
people.affiliation: Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press

people.name: Greg Veis
people.bio: Greg Veis is an executive editor of the Huffington Post Highline. Before that, he edited for The New Republic, The New York Times Magazine, and GQ.

people.name: Daniel Zwerdling
people.bio: Daniel Zwerdling, a correspondent in NPR’s Investigations Unit, has won some of the most prestigious awards in broadcasting. His career includes a stint as senior host of NPR’s Weekend All Things Considered, and a tour as NPR’s roving Africa correspondent based in Nairobi. Before joining NPR, Zwerdling was a staff writer at The New Republic.

Film screening venue is the National Portrait Gallery as printed on each film page. The film page header misprints the title as "(T)TERROR"; the schedule and synopsis say "(T)ERROR" (TOC: "(T)error"). 1971 (dir. Johanna Hamilton) is not in the films section; it screened inside the Oct 2 "Crossing Boundaries" session (p27) and is included as a film with only the facts printed there; its 3:00 PM time is the session start. The True Cost is labelled "Special Youth Screening" (put in slot). Spotlight is the "Opening Night Gala" film. Session times come from the day schedules on pp4-5 and descriptions from pp22-27. Printed typos normalised: "Dangerous Docs" 10:00am - 11:00pm -> 11:00 AM; "Meet the Funders" 11:00pm -> 11:00 AM. Where a session list and the schedule differ on moderators, the schedule was used: Access and Advocacy (Will Jenkins moderator, p4) and Meet the Funders (Caty Borum-Chattoo moderator, p5). Speaker names are normalised to the bio spelling in people[] arrays: "Bruce Brown" -> Bruce D. Brown, "Caty Borum-Chattoo" -> Caty Borum Chattoo, "Michael Schiller" -> Michael I. Schiller, "Matt Heineman" -> Matthew Heineman. Bio heading prints "DAN KRAUS" but the bio text and schedules say Krauss; Dan Krauss used. Alisia Essig's bio is cut off mid-sentence in the printed catalogue ("during both election"). Francesca Panetta (Storytelling on the Cutting Edge) and film discussants without bios have no people[] entry. The welcome letter (p8) states no theme.
